options: Awaiting `self.load()` twice in a row moves the first future, so the second call uses a value that was already consumed.
A default body cannot satisfy `+ Send` with an async block; it must be an `async fn` so the compiler infers `Send` automatically.
The default body's future keeps `&self` alive across an await, so it is `Send` only if the implementing type is `Sync`; the trait doesn't require `Sync`, so the promised `+ Send` can't be met.
The async block should be `async move`, because without `move` the block cannot borrow `self` across an await.
A default method cannot call another trait method that returns `impl Future`; it would have to be a required method.
MultipleChoice.prompt: A trait declares its async-style methods as returning `impl Future<Output = ...> + Send`, and gives one of them a default body. The trait has no supertraits. The code does not compile. Which line is the problem, and why?
reasons: Each call to `self.load()` creates a new future, and the first is dropped after its await completes. Nothing is reused or moved twice.

An `async fn` in a trait does not promise that its future is `Send`, so it would make the guarantee weaker, not stronger. Writing a plain `fn` that returns an async block is the way to keep the `Send` promise.

A future that holds `&Self` across an await is `Send` only when `Self: Sync`. The declared return type promises `Send` for every implementer, so the compiler rejects the default body. A `Send + Sync` supertrait on the trait, as the other async-returning traits in this codebase have, fixes it.
An async block may borrow `self` across an await. `async move` would still capture the same reference, so the `Send` problem would remain.
Default methods can call other methods of the trait, including ones that return `impl Future`. The failure is in the `Send` bound on the combined future, not in the call.

The declared return type promises `Send` for every implementer, so the compiler rejects the default body. A `Send + Sync` supertrait on the trait, as the other async-returning traits in this codebase have, fixes it.

MultipleChoice.prompt: This function checks that a submitted set of answers is valid before grading: every answer must refer to a question in the session, and there must be at most one answer per question. A test submitting two answers to the same question unexpectedly passes validation. Which version fixes it while keeping both checks?
reasons: Reordering the two checks changes nothing about the bug. The set is still re-created each iteration, so `insert` always succeeds and a repeated answer is never caught.
This only rewrites the membership test. The set is still created fresh on every iteration, so it is always empty when checked and duplicates still pass.

Comparing counts only catches duplicates when there are more answers than questions. Two answers to the same question in a session with several questions still pass, because the total stays within the limit.
The set of already-answered questions must live across iterations. Declared once before the loop, `insert` returns false the second time the same question appears, so a duplicate answer is rejected.

questions.explanation: The set of already-answered questions must live across iterations. Declared once before the loop, `insert` returns false the second time the same question appears, so a duplicate answer is rejected.

code.text:
let due = ["a", "b"];          // reviews due for the learner
let held = ["a"];              // asked by another pending session
let touched = ["a", "c"];      // concepts found in this change

let reviews: Vec<_> = due
    .iter()
    .filter(|id| !held.contains(id))
    .collect();
let new: Vec<_> = touched
    .iter()
    .filter(|id| !held.contains(id) && !reviews.contains(id))
    .collect();
println!("{reviews:?} {new:?}");

options: reviews is ["b"] and new is ["c"]
reviews is ["a", "b"] and new is ["c"]
reviews is ["b"] and new is []
reviews is ["b"] and new is ["a", "c"]
MultipleChoice.prompt: A learner has two due reviews, "a" and "b". Another of their pending sessions already asks "a", and the hold window has not expired. The learner now submits a change that touches concepts "a" and "c". The snippet mirrors how a session is composed. What does it print?
reasons: The held concept "a" is dropped from the reviews. It is also excluded from the asked-set used for new concepts, so the touched "a" is not asked in a second form. Only "b" as a review and "c" as a new concept remain.
This ignores the hold. A due review that another pending session already asks is left out of this session's reviews, so the scheduler does not count it twice.
This wrongly assumes that holding "a" blocks every new concept. The hold only affects the held concept. "c" is neither held nor due, so it is still asked as new.

This assumes the hold only filters the review list. If the held concept were not also in the asked-set, the touched "a" would come back as a new concept. The duplicate the hold prevents would just return by another route.

questions.explanation: The held concept "a" is dropped from the reviews. It is also excluded from the asked-set used for new concepts, so the touched "a" is not asked in a second form. Only "b" as a review and "c" as a new concept remain.

MultipleChoice.prompt: A learner has linked identities. Their learner store is reachable, and there are two organisation stores. The first organisation store holds a pending session of theirs, opened after the cutoff, covering concept X. While `held_concepts` is computing the held set, the second organisation store fails with an I/O error. What happens, and why is that the right design?
reasons: Only the learner store is tolerated, and only where organisation stores exist to cover for it. A failing organisation store may hold the very sessions that need to be held, so its error is propagated rather than hidden. ```
The code does no retrying. It reads each store once and either tolerates the error (learner store only) or returns it.
The function never discards the results of the stores it did read to compensate. A failure surfaces as an error, not as a misleading empty result.
Tolerance applies only to the learner store, which is read first. Skipping an organisation store would drop its held concepts and risk a duplicate question.

options: A `BTreeSet` of references cannot be queried with `contains`, because `&String` does not implement `Borrow<String>`.

The map step yields references into `due`, so the set borrows `due`. Consuming `due` with `into_iter` while that set is still used later is a borrow error. The ids need to be cloned into an owned set.
The set is built from `due.iter()`, so it is empty at runtime: `iter` only peeks at the elements and does not hand them to `collect`.
The filter closure receives a double reference, so `held.contains(*id)` cannot compile because it needs `**id`.
MultipleChoice.prompt: This code builds a set of the due ids that are already held elsewhere, then uses that set to filter the due list. It fails to compile. Which line is flawed, and why?
reasons: The standard library implements `Borrow<T>` for `&T`, so querying a set of `&String` with a `&String` compiles. The failure is that the set keeps `due` borrowed.

The set holds `&String` values that point into `due`. `due.into_iter()` moves `due` while `held_due` is still live in the filter, so the borrow checker rejects it. Cloning the ids, for example with `.cloned()` before `collect`, gives an owned `BTreeSet<String>` that does not borrow `due`.
`iter()` yields references that `collect` gathers into the set just as well. The code is rejected at compile time because of the borrow, so it never runs.
Here `id` in the filter is `&&String`, so `*id` is `&String`. That is exactly what `contains` expects, so this line is fine. The real problem is the lifetime of the borrowed elements.
